config.title: Build branded types for IDs

intro.title: Build branded types for IDs
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple user management system that uses TypeScript's branded types to create distinct, type-safe identifiers for different entities, like User IDs and Product IDs. You'll learn how branded types prevent mixing up different kinds of IDs at compile time, enhancing code safety. The core concepts involve using intersection types with a unique brand property to create these distinct types. You'll implement this by defining branded type aliases and using them in functions to ensure only the correct ID type is accepted.
intro.usecase: Branded types for IDs are essential in enterprise applications where multiple types of IDs must be distinguished at compile time. In e-commerce dashboards, you might have ProductID, OrderID, and UserID values that all look like strings but represent fundamentally different entities. TypeScript's structural typing would normally allow these to be mixed accidentally, but branded types prevent shipping an order with a user ID or displaying product details for an order ID. This pattern is commonly used in financial systems, inventory management interfaces, and customer relationship platforms where data integrity is critical.

objectives: Implement a branded type for a User ID using TypeScript's intersection types
Apply type assertions to convert primitive strings into branded ID types
Construct a function that validates and returns a branded ID from user input
Configure a function signature to accept only specific branded ID types as parameters
Manipulate existing code to replace primitive string IDs with branded types
Integrate branded ID types into a simple user profile object structure
Initialize variables with branded types and demonstrate type safety in assignments

steps.title: Import TypeScript utilities for branded types
steps.instruction: Import the TypeScript utilities that will be used throughout the lesson to create and work with branded types. Specifically, import the 'type' and 'interface' keywords from TypeScript's built-in types.
steps.hint: You don't need to install anything - these are TypeScript's built-in keywords. Just write the import statement at the top of the file.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: importing TypeScript utilities
import { type, interface } from 'typescript';

// Your code will go below

successCriteria: The 'type' and 'interface' keywords are imported from 'typescript'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to import both 'type' and 'interface' from 'typescript'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is incorrect. Remember to import 'type' and 'interface' from 'typescript'.

steps.title: Define a base branded type interface
steps.instruction: Create a generic Branded type interface that combines a base type with a unique brand property using TypeScript's intersection types.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' keyword to define a generic type that intersects a base type with an object containing a brand property.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: Generic branded type
type Branded<T, Brand> = T & { readonly __brand: Brand };
steps.expectedOutcome: A generic Branded type is defined that can be used to create branded types for IDs.
successCriteria: A generic Branded type is created using intersection types with a brand property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your Branded type is generic and uses intersection types with a brand property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Branded type definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to create a generic type that intersects a base type with a unique brand property.

steps.title: Create a UserId branded type
steps.instruction: Define a UserId type using the Branded interface with string as the base type.
steps.hint: Use the Branded interface you defined earlier to create a specific type for user IDs.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: another branded type for Order IDs
type OrderId = Branded<string, 'OrderId'>;
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a UserId type that is a branded string, preventing accidental mixing with other string IDs.
successCriteria: UserId type is defined using Branded<string, 'UserId'>
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the Branded interface correctly with string as the base type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The UserId type wasn't defined correctly. Remember to use the Branded interface with string as the base type.
